paras: The lynching of Peter Stamps took place at Douglasville, Georgia, in late July 1885, when a mob reported at 500 men took Stamps, a Black man, from custody and hanged him at a railroad bridge. Stamps had been jailed after Ida Abercrombie, the daughter of a white farmer, named him as the father of her expected child, and the mob formed after she died in convulsions. Newspapers across the country carried the case as a one-line brief, while the fullest dispatch added that strychnine was found in the girl's body and that her death might have been suicide.

According to an Atlanta dispatch dated July 25, Stamps worked on the place of a 'well-to-do white farmer' whose daughter, Ida Abercrombie, was discovered by her parents two days earlier to be pregnant. The dispatch reported that she named Stamps as the father and said he had outraged her a year before and had compelled her to submit since. Stamps was arrested and placed in jail. Briefs in other papers gave the girl's age as thirteen.

On the day before the lynching, the girl told her father she was going to die and died in convulsions before help could be found. A mob then organized, and that night Stamps was taken from the sheriff, who was trying to get him out of the county, and was hanged from the railroad bridge. The Cleveland Gazette said instead that he was taken from the jail.

The same dispatch reported that Stamps had said the girl consented, that a post mortem found strychnine in her stomach, and that her child was 'colored'. It closed by noting 'great excitement' over her death and calling it 'a mystery' whether she had committed suicide.
No report of an inquest into Stamps's death, of any arrest of mob members, or of official action appears in the coverage.

Most papers reduced the case to a single sentence in a news or crime column, such as the Superior Times's 'Minor News Notes', the Watertown Republican's 'Deeds of Blood' and 'The Criminal Calendar' in two Dakota weeklies. These briefs said Stamps was lynched for 'an assault on a girl of 13' or for an 'alleged rape' of Ida Abercrombie, and they made no mention of the poisoning. The Superior Times printed its brief twice, on August 1 and again on August 8.

The Rugby Gazette and East Tennessee News gave a different version without names, stating that 'a negro committed a terrible outrage' on a 'highly respectable young white girl' who 'died next day'. It described the lynchers as 'a mob composed of leading citizens of the county'. By contrast, the Weekly Arizona Miner, which ran the Atlanta dispatch under the headline 'Revolting Chapter', called the rape 'alleged' and printed the strychnine finding and the question of suicide.

The Cleveland Gazette carried the case in 'Relative to Our People the Country Over', a column of news about Black Americans, as a single unadorned line saying Stamps was lynched 'for outraging a little white girl'. No other coverage in the Black press, and no Georgia newspaper account, appears among the reports found.

The date of the lynching differs: the Atlanta dispatch of July 25 placed it 'last night', while the Watertown Republican gave the night of the 25th. Accounts also differ on the girl's death, which the Rugby Gazette tied to the outrage and the Atlanta dispatch to strychnine and possible suicide.

reader.title: Lynching of Peter Stamps
bases: A mob seized Peter Stamps, a Black man accused of assaulting a white girl, from jail or from the sheriff and hanged him (A1, A7, A10).
Every report says Stamps was 'lynched' by a mob, given as 500 men, after he was taken from custody (A1, A7, A10); the mob acted on an accusation of rape or assault on a white girl (A2, A10).

Several separately worded reports agree that Stamps was lynched by a mob at Douglasville for an alleged assault on a girl (A1, A2, A4, A7, A10), though all appear to derive from telegraph news and none is a local Georgia paper.

accounts.label: Atlanta dispatch (July 25)
accounts.gist: The girl was found to be pregnant, named Stamps, and died in convulsions; a mob of 500 took Stamps from the sheriff and hanged him at the railroad bridge. It adds that Stamps said she consented, that strychnine was found, that her child was 'colored', and that suicide was possible.

accounts.gist: An unnamed negro committed 'a terrible outrage' on a young white girl who died next day; he was captured and lynched by leading citizens of the county.

framing.detail: The Rugby Gazette states the 'terrible outrage' as fact, calls the girl 'highly respectable', and describes the mob as 'leading citizens of the county'.
The Weekly Arizona Miner's 'Revolting Chapter' says 'alleged' rape, prints Stamps's claim of consent and the strychnine finding, and calls the girl's death a mystery.
Wisconsin, Minnesota and Dakota weeklies ran one-sentence briefs in crime columns such as 'Deeds of Blood' and 'The Criminal Calendar'.
The Cleveland Gazette ran a one-line item, without comment, in its column of news about 'our people'.

Douglasville (also printed Douglassville and Douglass), Georgia; hanged at the railroad bridge
